HOME_TITLE: Kmila-9s: A Multiplatform VHDL Learning and Debugging Tool
HOME_SUBTITLE: An application for learning and debugging VHDL code without requiring physical hardware.
HOME_OVERVIEW_P1: Kmila-9s is a multiplatform desktop application, running in a local environment, aimed at debugging VHDL (VHSIC Hardware Description Language) code. Its objective is to facilitate the analysis of programs through simulation and interactive visualization of digital signals, clock cycles, and port states.
HOME_OVERVIEW_P2: The project aims to support the academic learning of digital design for FPGAs (Field Programmable Gate Arrays), offering a free and open-source tool that strengthens educational practices and allows for a practical understanding of the logic of digital systems without requiring physical hardware.
HOME_FEATURE_VISUALIZATION_DESC: Observe the states of signals, ports, and internal variables at any time.
HOME_FEATURE_CROSSPLATFORM_DESC: Runs on Windows, macOS, Android, iOS, iPadOS, and Linux (via web).
HOME_FEATURE_OFFLINE_DESC: Works locally without an internet connection.
HOME_FEATURE_PRELAB_DESC: Prepare for physical lab sessions in advance.
HOME_FEATURE_ACCESSIBILITY_DESC: Study from any computer or mobile device.
HOME_FEATURE_PROTOTYPING_DESC: Validate designs faster than with traditional methods.

GATE_AND_SUMMARY: Output is 1 only when every input is 1.
GATE_AND_DESC: Boolean conjunction. The output reflects the logical AND of its inputs (y = a · b). Used to detect when multiple conditions are simultaneously true — e.g. gating a signal with an enable, masking specific bits of a vector, or building wider logic.
GATE_NAND_SUMMARY: Inverted AND: output is 0 only when every input is 1.
GATE_NAND_DESC: Logical NAND (NOT AND). The bubble at the output flips an AND's result. Notable property: NAND is universal — any other gate can be built out of NANDs alone, which is why CMOS standard-cell libraries usually have NAND as the densest primitive.
GATE_OR_SUMMARY: Output is 1 when any input is 1.
GATE_OR_DESC: Boolean disjunction (y = a + b). Used to merge signals — "this OR that" — and to build alarm / event logic. Like NAND, NOR is also universal, but OR by itself is one of the two basic Boolean operators.
GATE_NOR_SUMMARY: Inverted OR: output is 1 only when every input is 0.
GATE_NOR_DESC: Logical NOR (NOT OR). Universal, like NAND — any logic can be built from NORs alone. Common in standard-cell libraries and in hardware where inverting outputs is naturally free (CMOS).
GATE_XOR_SUMMARY: Output is 1 when exactly one input is 1.
GATE_XOR_DESC: Logical exclusive OR — true when the inputs differ (y = a ⊕ b). Building block for adders (sum bit), parity checkers, encryption (one-time-pad XOR), and bit-flipping. An XOR with one input tied to 1 acts as a controllable inverter.
GATE_XNOR_SUMMARY: Output is 1 when both inputs are equal.
GATE_XNOR_DESC: Logical exclusive NOR — true when the inputs match (y = a ≡ b). Useful as a per-bit equality test; an XNOR over each bit followed by an AND across results gives vector-equality (the EQ comparator we synthesise from the `=` operator).
GATE_NOT_SUMMARY: Output is the logical inverse of the input.
GATE_NOT_DESC: Single-input gate. y = ¬a — flips 0 to 1 and 1 to 0. The smallest Boolean primitive. Used to build everything from NAND/NOR by combining with AND/OR; in active-low interfaces (reset_n, write_enable_n) the inverter is what makes the polarity work out.
GATE_BUF_DESC: Single-input cell that just forwards its input (y = a). In real silicon, buffers exist to drive long wires (signal restoration), to sit in a fan-out tree, or to add a small deliberate delay. In our schematic, BUFs are emitted whenever an internal gate's output needs to be "renamed" onto a declared port or signal — they make the connection between the gate and the named net visible as a wire.
GATE_BUF_NOTE: BUFs are hidden in the Synthesis and Debug views — there they're folded away and the wire goes directly from the driving gate to the target port. Naive view keeps them so the source-line groupings stay literal.
GATE_MUX_SUMMARY: Picks one of several inputs based on a selector.
GATE_MUX_DESC: Two-input MUX: y = s ? d1 : d0. Wider MUXes select among 2^n inputs with n select bits. Multiplexers implement decision logic — every `if/then/else` and `case` statement in VHDL becomes a MUX (or a tree of them) after synthesis. They're also how registers implement load-enable: the MUX picks between "new value" and "hold" based on the enable signal.
GATE_DFF_SUMMARY: Stores one bit, sampled on the active clock edge.
GATE_DFF_DESC: Edge-triggered storage element. On each rising edge of CLK, the value at D is captured and held at Q until the next edge. Between edges Q is stable regardless of D activity. Foundational building block of synchronous design — every register, every pipeline stage, every state machine state-bit is one or more DFFs. Combine with a MUX in front of D to get an enabled register; with a 2-input MUX selecting `'0' / D` to get a synchronous reset.
GATE_DFF_NOTE: The Edge attribute on this cell tells you whether it samples on rising_edge or falling_edge.
GATE_CONST_SUMMARY: Fixed value driver — '0', '1', or a literal vector.
GATE_CONST_DESC: Constant nets show up as small labels rather than gates. Common in synthesis output: every `'0'`, `'1'`, `"0000"`, or `(others => '0')` literal in the source becomes a constant-driver net. Tying a MUX input to a constant is how synchronous reset paths are built (`d <= '0' when reset = '1' else next_value`).
GATE_ADD_DESC: Renders the `+` operator. Internally, an adder is a chain of full-adders (XOR for the sum bit, AND/OR for the carry), but we keep it as one opaque cell by default — an 8-bit ripple-carry adder is ~50 gates and would dominate the diagram. The exporter's "expand arithmetic" toggle (planned) breaks this down to gates.
GATE_SUB_DESC: Renders the `-` operator. Built from an adder plus a row of NOTs and a carry-in of 1 (two's complement: a − b = a + (¬b) + 1). Kept opaque for the same reason as ADD.
GATE_MUL_DESC: Renders the `*` operator. Multipliers in hardware are large structures (an n×n multiplier is roughly n² half-adders). Often mapped to dedicated DSP slices on FPGAs rather than synthesised as logic gates.
GATE_DIV_DESC: Renders the `/` operator. Hardware division is expensive and slow — many designs avoid it or restrict it to multi-cycle operations.
GATE_MOD_DESC: Renders the `mod` operator. Hardware-wise this is essentially a divider that exposes the remainder. Cheap when the divisor is a power of two (just slice off the low bits).
GATE_POW_DESC: Renders the `**` operator. Rare in synthesisable VHDL; usually only seen with constant exponents (which the synthesiser unrolls into a chain of multipliers).
GATE_SHL_SUMMARY: Shifts the input vector left by N bits.
GATE_SHL_DESC: VHDL `sll` (logical) fills with 0; `sla` (arithmetic) fills with the rightmost bit. Equivalent to multiplication by 2^N when the shift amount is a constant. Implemented in hardware as a barrel shifter (a tree of 2-to-1 MUXes).
GATE_SHR_SUMMARY: Shifts the input vector right by N bits.
GATE_SHR_DESC: VHDL `srl` (logical) fills with 0; `sra` (arithmetic) fills with the sign bit. Equivalent to integer division by 2^N for unsigned (`srl`) or signed (`sra`) values.
GATE_ROL_SUMMARY: Cyclically rotates the input vector left.
GATE_ROL_DESC: Bits shifted off the left wrap back into the right end — no bits are lost. Common in cryptographic primitives and CRC computation.
GATE_ROR_SUMMARY: Cyclically rotates the input vector right.
GATE_ROR_DESC: Mirror of ROL — bits off the right wrap into the left.
GATE_EQ_SUMMARY: Outputs 1 when both inputs are equal.
GATE_EQ_DESC: Per-bit XNOR followed by an AND across all the bits. For 1-bit inputs, this is just an XNOR. We emit EQ cells when synthesising `case`/`with-select` statements — each `when` choice becomes an EQ comparator against the selector.
GATE_NEQ_DESC: Inverse of EQ — equivalent to a per-bit XOR followed by an OR.
GATE_LT_DESC: Magnitude comparator. Built from a chain of full-adder-style cells in hardware; we keep it as a single opaque cell.
GATE_LTE_DESC: Same family as LT, with a tweaked carry-out interpretation.
GATE_BLACKBOX_SUMMARY: A VHDL process whose body the synthesiser couldn't decompose.
GATE_BLACKBOX_DESC: Process bodies that use loops, function calls, or constructs we don't lower yet end up rendered as a single opaque cell. Inputs come from the sensitivity list; outputs are the signals the body assigns. The diagnostics row at the top of the schematic explains why each blackbox showed up.
GATE_BLACKBOX_NOTE: Future synthesiser iterations will decompose more of these — see the synthesis-coverage roadmap.
SCHEMATIC_ATTR_REASON_BLACKBOX_GENERIC: Process body uses constructs not yet decomposed (loops / function calls / etc.).
